title: Your chats on every device — what you want, before anything is built

steps.path: Any chat, on your laptop, desktop or phone
steps.headline: Which of these must be true before you would call this done?
steps.today: Each device keeps its own copy of every chat. A backup folder carries copies between them, after a reply finishes and with a short delay.
steps.problem: The draft design promises six different things at once. Building all six is months of work; building the two you care about is weeks.
steps.proposal: Pick everything that must be true. Anything unpicked can come later or never.

options.label: Never lose a message
pros: Every message you send or receive ends up on every device, no matter which one you quit or when.
cons: On its own it changes nothing you see; it only stops things going missing.

options.label: Pick up on any device
pros: Sit down at any device and your next message simply works, with no warnings or buttons.
cons: Needs a rule for who is in charge of a chat, which is where today's warnings come from.

options.label: Watch a reply live elsewhere
pros: Your phone shows the desktop's reply appearing word by word.
cons: Both devices must be on and reachable at the same moment; it does nothing for a device that was off.

options.label: Phone works when computers are off
pros: Chats keep going from anywhere, with no computer awake at home.
cons: The phone has none of your project files, so project chats would behave differently there.

steps.headline: Which devices should this cover?
steps.today: Your backup space has copies from this laptop, the desktop PC, an older Windows laptop and the phone.
steps.problem: Every extra kind of device adds cases to design for. A device you no longer use still shows up in warnings and copies.
steps.proposal: Pick every device that should take part. The rest can read chats but never run them.

options.label: This laptop
options.summary: The Linux laptop you are reading this on.

options.label: The desktop PC
options.summary: The Linux desktop that held the lost messages on Nov 5.

options.label: The Windows laptop
options.summary: The Galaxy Book; its last copies are from July.

steps.path: A chat with a project folder attached
steps.headline: When a chat moves to another device, what else must move with it?
steps.today: A chat is a list of messages. Behind it sit the project folder's files, any programs the assistant left running, and the undo history of its edits.
steps.problem: Messages alone can move easily. Files, running programs and undo history live on one machine and cannot simply follow.
steps.proposal: Pick what must travel. Anything unpicked stays on the device it was made on, and the assistant is told so.

options.label: The messages
pros: Cheap to carry; this is what sync does today.
cons: None.

options.label: Edited project files
pros: The other device sees the same code and documents the assistant changed.
cons: Needs the project folder on both devices, kept in step by its own sync. Big folders are slow.

options.label: Programs still running
pros: A long build or test keeps going.
cons: Not possible to move; the best you can get is a note saying where it is running.

options.label: Undo history
pros: Undo works on the new device for edits made on the old one.
cons: Only meaningful if the edited files also moved.

steps.page: Being on two devices at once
steps.intro: The first page said what matters. These decide what you see when two devices look at the same chat.

steps.path: The chat window on a second device
steps.headline: A reply is running on your desktop. You open the same chat on your laptop. What should you see?
steps.today: The laptop shows its last copy, which may be a few minutes old, and a warning that the desktop may have newer messages.
steps.problem: You cannot tell whether the desktop is still working, and typing on the laptop creates a second, separate version of the chat.
steps.proposal: Pick what the laptop should show while the desktop is mid-reply.

options.label: Watch, and type ahead
pros: You see the reply appear live and your typed message is sent as soon as the reply ends.
Nothing is ever lost or duplicated.
cons: Live watching only works while both devices are on and reachable; otherwise you see a notice instead.

options.label: Watch only
pros: Simplest to understand: the chat is read-only until the desktop finishes.
cons: You have to wait and remember to come back before you can type.

options.label: A notice, no live view
pros: Nothing new to build for watching; a line says Desktop is replying.
cons: You cannot see what the desktop is doing or whether it is stuck.

steps.path: Any chat open on two devices
steps.headline: Should the reply stay on the device it started on, or follow you as you move?
steps.today: Nothing moves. Each device runs its own copy, and the copies collide later.
steps.problem: Moving a reply mid-thought stops it, restarts it elsewhere, and makes the assistant re-read the whole chat. Not moving it means your laptop sends messages to the desktop to run.
steps.proposal: Pick where the thinking should happen when you switch devices.

options.label: Stays put until a quiet moment
pros: Replies never stop halfway.
Your message from the laptop is run by the desktop and the answer appears on both.
cons: If the desktop is slow or busy, your laptop waits on it.

options.label: Follows you at once
pros: The device you are typing on always does the work.
cons: The running reply is cut off and restarted.
Every switch re-reads the whole chat: a slower first reply and more of your plan allowance used.

options.label: You choose each time
pros: Full control.
cons: A question to answer every time you change seats.

steps.headline: Both devices added messages to the same chat without knowing. What should happen to the two versions?
steps.today: The bigger file wins and the smaller becomes a conflict copy in the folder, which the app never shows you. That is how the Nov 5 messages vanished.
steps.problem: Your own folder shows this is rare: of 26 leftover copies, 23 held nothing unique. Only 3 were real splits, but those 3 held lost messages.
steps.proposal: Pick what the app should do with a real split.

options.label: Keep both as separate chats
pros: Nothing is lost and nothing is invented.
Each version reads exactly as it happened.
cons: Two entries in your chat list named the same, with a note saying which device made which.

options.label: Stitch into one chat
pros: One entry in the list, all messages in time order.
cons: The assistant would see messages it never answered, and undo history can break.
Nobody has proven Claude Code reads a stitched file correctly.

options.label: Ask me each time
pros: You decide.
cons: A dialog about files you did not know existed, at a moment you were trying to work.

steps.path: A chat whose other device has not uploaded yet
steps.headline: A device quit before uploading its last messages. What should the other device say when you open that chat?
steps.today: Nothing. The chat opens looking complete, and your next message starts a split.
steps.problem: Upload at quit gets 6 seconds; your long chat took about 35. The lost Nov 5 messages were exactly this.
steps.proposal: The quitting device could send a tiny note, in under a second, saying it holds unsent messages. Pick what the other device does with that note.

options.label: Warn, but let me type
pros: You know the chat is behind and can wake the other device, or carry on anyway.
cons: Carrying on makes a split, kept as two chats per the question above.

options.label: Warn and lock typing
pros: No split can happen.
cons: A chat you cannot type into until a device that may be in a bag at the office comes online.

options.label: Say nothing
pros: No new notice to read.
cons: Today's behaviour, with its lost messages.

steps.intro: A lid shuts, wifi drops, a battery dies. These decide what happens to a reply that was running there.

steps.path: A chat whose reply was running on a device that went offline
steps.headline: The desktop goes offline mid-reply. What should the other devices do?
steps.today: Nothing. The reply is simply cut off on the desktop and no other device knows it was running.
steps.problem: A device that looks dead may only be on bad wifi and still working. Two devices doing the same job can send messages, edit files or run commands twice.
steps.proposal: Pick what the other devices should do, about a minute and a half after the desktop stops answering.

options.label: Show a Continue here button
pros: You see the cut-off reply marked Desktop went offline and carry on with one tap, or wait for the desktop.
cons: A long unattended job stalls until you notice.

options.label: Continue automatically elsewhere
pros: Long jobs carry on by themselves.
cons: If the desktop was only on bad wifi, two devices now do the same work and duplicates cannot be undone.
The whole chat is re-read on the new device.

options.label: Wait for the desktop
pros: Never a duplicate.
cons: Your chat is stuck until that device returns, even if it is dead for good.

steps.path: A chat whose reply was cut off
steps.headline: When a cut-off reply continues on another device, should it finish the old reply or start fresh from your last message?
steps.problem: Half a reply may have already edited files or run commands on the old device. The new device does not have those results.
steps.proposal: Pick what the new device does with the half-finished work.

options.label: Start fresh, with a note
pros: The assistant is told the previous attempt was cut off on another device and what it had said so far, and decides how to proceed.
cons: It may redo steps the old device completed.

options.label: Resume exactly where it stopped
pros: No repeated work.
cons: Not safely possible: the new device cannot see what the old one's half-done commands did.

options.label: Drop the half reply
pros: Clean slate; you ask again.
cons: Whatever the old device said before the cut is hidden from you.

steps.headline: Should a device upload its unsent messages when it goes to sleep, not only when you quit?
steps.today: Closing the lid does nothing. Messages wait until the next finished reply or until you quit, and quit allows only 6 seconds.
steps.problem: A laptop that sleeps in a bag holds messages no other device can see, sometimes for days.
steps.proposal: Yes means closing the lid triggers an upload first, so the laptop may stay awake a few extra seconds. No leaves sleep as it is. Don't know parks it.

steps.intro: The phone has no project folder and Android can freeze the app at any time. These decide what it is for.

steps.headline: What should the phone be able to do with your chats?
steps.today: The phone runs the same engine as the desktop. It can run any chat on its own, or connect to one computer and show that computer's chats instead.
steps.problem: Running on the phone uses its battery and data, Android may freeze the app mid-reply, and project files are not there.
steps.proposal: Pick everything the phone should do. Anything unpicked, the phone simply does not offer.

options.label: Read every chat
pros: Catch up anywhere.
cons: None.

options.label: Send a message a computer runs
pros: Your desktop does the work with all its files; the phone shows the answer.
cons: Needs a computer awake; otherwise the message waits.

options.label: Watch a computer's reply live
pros: See progress on a long job from the sofa.
cons: Needs both on and reachable at that moment.

options.label: Run chats with no project folder
pros: General chats keep working with every computer off.
cons: Battery, data, and Android freezing the app mid-reply.

options.label: Run project chats too
pros: Never blocked.
cons: The assistant cannot see or edit the project's files, so it may answer wrongly or claim edits that did not happen.

steps.path: A project chat on the phone, with every computer off
steps.headline: With both computers off, you send a message to a project chat from the phone. What should happen?
steps.today: The phone runs it itself, without the project's files.
steps.problem: The assistant may answer as if the files were there, or try to edit files that do not exist on the phone.
steps.proposal: Pick what the phone should do with that message.

options.label: Queue it for a computer
pros: It runs properly the moment a computer wakes, and the phone shows Will run when Desktop wakes.
cons: No answer until then.

options.label: Run it, with a warning
pros: You get an answer now.
cons: The warning is easy to miss, and a wrong answer about files you cannot see is worse than waiting.

options.label: Ask me each time
pros: You decide per message.
cons: One more tap on every message sent from the phone.

steps.headline: Should the phone download every chat, or only the list plus what you open?
steps.today: The phone downloads the whole backup space the same way a computer does. Yours is about 9 GB of chats plus 10 GB of history, and 25 chats are too big to sync at all.
steps.problem: A full download on a phone is slow, uses data, and gets worse every month.
steps.proposal: Pick how much the phone should hold.

options.label: The list, then what you open
pros: The list appears in seconds; a chat downloads when you tap it.
Fixes the 25 chats that never sync today.
cons: A chat is unreadable offline until you have opened it once.
Bigger change: the backup needs a separate small list alongside the chat files.

options.label: Everything, as today
pros: Every chat readable offline.
cons: Gigabytes on the phone, slow first setup, 25 chats still missing.

options.label: The last 30 days
pros: Small and fast; recent chats offline.
cons: Older chats are simply absent on the phone.

steps.intro: How fast live has to be, what a switch costs, and what gets built first.

steps.path: A chat watched from a second device
steps.headline: How live does live need to be?
steps.today: Other devices see a reply only after it finishes and the backup carries it, usually within a minute.
steps.problem: Word by word needs a direct connection between the two devices at that moment, over your private network. Every few seconds through the backup folder would bloat it badly.
steps.proposal: Pick the speed you would notice and want.

options.label: Word by word when connected
pros: Feels like one chat on two screens.
The connection piece already exists for the phone.
cons: Works only when both devices are on your private network at once; otherwise falls back to when it finishes.

options.label: When the reply finishes
pros: Nothing new to connect; works through the backup folder from anywhere.
cons: A long reply is invisible elsewhere until it ends.

steps.path: Any chat you continue on a different device
steps.headline: Switching devices makes the assistant re-read the whole chat. How should the app treat that cost?
steps.today: Every device re-reads from scratch anyway, because each runs its own copy.
steps.problem: The assistant's saved reading of a chat lives on the device that made it and lasts about an hour on your plan. A switch within that hour means a slower first reply and more of your allowance spent, about a dollar's worth on a very long chat.
steps.proposal: Pick how the app should behave about it.

options.label: Prefer the device that was last replying
pros: While that device is reachable, it keeps doing the work and nothing is re-read; you just type from wherever you are.
cons: Depends on that device staying awake and online.

options.label: Switch freely, say nothing
pros: Simplest rule: the device you type on does the work.
cons: Slower first reply after each switch, and the extra cost is invisible to you.

options.label: Switch freely, show a small note
pros: You see Re-reading this chat when it happens.
cons: One more line of status to read; the cost is the same.

steps.headline: Which piece should be built and shown to you first?
steps.today: The draft design lists five steps in one order: stop losing messages, one list everywhere, device handoff, live view, phone fallback.
steps.problem: Each step is weeks of work and each changes what you see. The order decides what improves first.
steps.proposal: Pick the first piece. The rest get their own decks later, in the order you set then.

options.label: Stop losing messages
pros: Fixes the Nov 5 problem and the false warnings; everything else builds on it.
Smallest piece, and your own folder shows it would have settled 23 of 26 conflicts.
cons: Nothing new to see beyond fewer warnings.

options.label: Live view
pros: The most visible change.
cons: Built on today's copying, it would still lose messages underneath.

options.label: Automatic handoff
pros: Sitting down anywhere just works.
cons: Needs the who-is-online piece first, which does not exist yet.

options.label: Phone without computers
pros: Chats from anywhere.
cons: Only safe once the handoff rules exist.

steps.path: Your backup folder's leftover conflict copies
steps.headline: Should the two lost Nov 5 exchanges be put back into their chat now, before any of this is built?
steps.today: They sit in two conflict copies in your backup folder, which the app never shows. One holds lets switch. sure its safe? and the other holds okay i think we're good? with its reply.
steps.problem: They stay invisible until the new system exists, which is weeks away.
steps.proposal: Yes means a one-off repair, shown to you for approval before anything is written, that adds each as a separate chat named after its device. No leaves them where they are. Don't know parks it.

steps.headline: Is there anything this system must never do, or anything you pictured that no question above covered?
steps.today: The questions above cover what I understood from the draft design and your folder.
steps.problem: A rule you hold in your head and never said is the one most likely to be broken.
steps.proposal: Write it in a line or two. It becomes a rule the design is checked against.
steps.prompt: e.g. never move a reply without telling me
